Why do 'free' eye tests end up costing customers extra?
Evidence: Stated free care, Bundled OCT charges, Hidden upgrade fees
#Aletheia #ConsumerRights

Promotions and government entitlements suggest eye tests are entirely free for eligible medical card and PRSI holders.
Stated Judgement: (+1.0, 0.0) — Good Preference

Customers face unexpected baseline charges because mandatory diagnostic scans like OCT are quietly bundled into standard appointments.
Resulting Judgement: (-1.0, -0.9) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. Marketing promises free care while administrative bundling quietly extracts baseline fees from consumers.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Promotional Messaging: FAIL (-0.85, -0.80) — Promotes free tests while omitting bundled fees.
- Point-of-Sale Transparency: FAIL (-0.85, -0.85) — Opaque pricing and unexpected add-ons at checkout.
Irish customers frequently report unexpected charges during routine visits, as mandatory advanced scans inflate baseline costs past advertised rates.

The Bright Side:
Advanced scans provide genuine clinical value for early detection, provided patients are fully informed in advance.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing promotional eligibility (WHO qualifies) with retail checkout realities (WHAT is actually charged).

Social Physics Analysis:
Specsavers runs a classic Smart Selfish Maneuver: using alluring zero-cost promotional hooks to drive foot traffic, then extracting margin via mandatory bundled diagnostic add-ons at checkout.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Marketing pretexts mask profit extraction behind mandatory medical bundling.

The Unavoidable Truth: Promotional healthcare claims often conceal mandatory service bundling.

The Unavoidable Lie: Eye tests are completely free without hidden diagnostic costs.

Alethekanon:
Marketing claims of absolute zero-cost access collapse when routine appointments require bundled diagnostic fees.

Awwthekanon:
It is frustrating when you step into a healthcare appointment expecting a straightforward, covered service, only to receive a surprise bill at the end because extra scans were bundled in without clear prior notice.

Brothekanon:
Classic retail move right there. Big sign says free, you sit in the chair, and suddenly there's a surprise €25 scan tacked on before you can even blink.

Spirithekanon:
"Better is little with righteousness than great revenues without right." Proverbs 16:8 PASS
Transparent dealings nourish trust, whereas hidden fees erode community faith for fleeting gain.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Eye tests are supposed to be free, so why does Specsavers charge for them?

Many Irish customers have complained about upselling in Specsavers – but ‘advanced’ eye tests may be a good idea for some.

Actual Article Body:
Sign in. It’s quick, free and it’s up to you.

An account is an optional way to support the work we do. Find out more.

RYANAIR GETS A bad rap for all the extra charges its website pushes at you between choosing your flight and paying for it.

Some opticians could probably give Ryanair a run for its money. It’s not unusual to come away with your new glasses with the uneasy feeling that you have paid quite a bit more than expected.

A quick skim of the Google reviews of Irish branches of Specsavers from the past year reveals numerous customers complaining they were charged far more for lenses than they expected, or feeling they had been subjected to multiple “upsells”.

“I came in to get new glasses and sunglasses in the 2-for-1 deal, but somehow the total came to way, way more than I was expecting,” says one review of Specsavers on Dawson Street from a customer who was shocked to find she was being charged €120 for lenses on top of the price of frames “with no clear breakdown as to why”.

“The pricing was very opaque and there were numerous attempts to upsell,” another writes.

There are also many positive online reviews on Specsavers’ Irish branches, of which there are over 60, praising the friendliness and professionalism of the staff, and the company seems to be hearing all the negative feedback – it writes back to bad reviews asking for more information so it can “take a closer look”.

But is it listening?

Part of the problem is the way prices are advertised and displayed in opticians. It’s standard for frames to have one price displayed, but for the person selling you the glasses to strongly recommend various add-ons for the lenses – scratch resistance and anti-glare treatments and so on – that ramp up the final figure.

In some branches of Specsavers, unlike in other chains such as Vision Express and trendy recent entrant to the Irish market Ace & Tate, lens options are not displayed prominently on the shop floor alongside the frames.

Nowhere is this price confusion more problematic than when it comes to eye tests.

That’s because if you’re paying pay-related social insurance (PRSI) or have a medical card, you’re entitled to a free eye test every two years. This is also something that Specsavers itself advertises.

A large LED screen outside Specsavers on Henry Street in Dublin asks: “Why not add ‘get an eye test’ to today’s shopping list?” and goes on to state that “a lot of eye test” – including optic nerve assessment, retinal health examination, and astigmatic correction – is available “for €0 with PRSI or medical card, €30 without”.

However, when The Journal went into this branch to ask how much an eye test was, the answer given was €55. What if you have PRSI? Then, the staff member said, it’s €25.

When this journalist actually got an eye test in another Dublin branch of Specsavers last month, the charge was indeed €25, with no option of a free test presented at the point of sale.

Irish customers both with and without medical cards have complained of being charged €25 for eye tests in Specsavers.

“Both government and their own site say free PRSI treatment, but they still find a way to charge you €25 once you’re booked in,” states one recent review of Specsavers on Opera Lane in Cork city.

Advertisement

“My PRSI eye test cost me €25. They added a test without informing me,” states a review of Specsavers in Blanchardstown in Dublin.

So what’s going on? The discrepancy between the free test people are entitled to and the price Specsavers is charging is caused by the fact that the company is performing something called an optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan as standard as part of its eye tests, and that costs extra.

Some independent opticians also provide an OCT, some don’t. Vision Express does it – but the price is only €10, which is quite a bit less than Specsavers’ €25.

So is an OCT scan something we need?

Declan
